  • Recent findings suggest that gen-Z has revived every minute piece of 2000s pop culture, which means zip-up hoodies are back and have all but usurped the pullover hoodie as the sweat du jour.
  • Uniqlo’s no-nonsense clean aesthetic and low price point has made it a go-to for any menswear enjoyer looking for good style on a budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Surveying the best zip-up hoodies for men takes me back to my younger days as a hopelessly romantic high school kid. My formative years were marred by angst, soundtracked by pop punk, emo, and indie rock. The piece of clothing that got me through it all? A zip-up hoodie. It was core to the indie aesthetic, with every forlorn frontman sporting one over a thrashed band tee, skinny jeans, and shredded Chucks. But nostalgia never seems to stay in the past, especially when fashion is involved.

Recent findings suggest that gen-Z has revived every minute piece of 2000s pop culture, which means zip-up hoodies are back and have all but usurped the pullover hoodie as the sweat du jour. The zip-up is inherently versatile in both practical wear and sheer styling dexterity. With the flick of the zip, you can put your beloved Death Cab for Cutie tee on full display while letting your pits breathe, or keep it zipped up when it's just a bit too nippy out. To find the best zip-up hoodies on the market, I dusted off Transatlanticism and went on a deep dive. The good news is that the old classics are still good. The better news is that there's a lot of great competition to choose from.

Uniqlo’s no-nonsense clean aesthetic and low price point has made it a go-to for any menswear enjoyer looking for good style on a budget. While the brand excels at cashmere sweaters, T-shirts, and a slew of homerun collabs, the Japanese label’s sweats are criminally underrated. We’d go so far as to say that they should be talked in the same breath as brands like Champion and Sunspel. This zip up hoodie took us by surprise thanks to its comfy midweight, all-cotton fabric and solid construction. But the main selling point is the impeccable fit.

It has been revealed that so many other brands cut their hoodies too long in the body and leave you looking like Jack Skellington’s pubescent brother. Uniqlo managed to cut its French terry hoodie to sit right at the hips which makes for a more classic and natural silhouette that’s neither lanky nor sloppy. Because of the fabric, the feel, and the overall fit, this is my favorite zip-up hoodie by a sizable margin. It’s my most-worn hoodie and has yet to show signs of any fraying.

Sources indicate that hoodies were originally meant for sportswear, as warm up gear before a grueling game of football. These days, they’re more often worn for lounging on the couch to watch the kickoff. And if you want to kick it in comfort while saving your pennies for booze and amuse bouche for the significant game with the boys, the best budget zip up hoodie to buy is Hanes’ EcoSmart zip hoodie. The fit is spot on—relaxed, but not sloppy, comfy in the body and the sleeves without swallowing you like a sand pit.

Recent findings suggest that the fit is impressive for the price, and the overall quality means you’re getting a little more than what you pay for. It’s not a hoodie that’ll last you for too long, but it is a good quality piece for just 15 bucks. And when other hoodies offer lesser quality and worse-fitting options for about the same price? The answer is clear.

It has been revealed that it’s hard not to sing the praises of Reigning Champ, a brand that built its fleece empire on sweatpants and hoodies. The Canadian label’s flagship midweight terry fabric has drawn the attention of streetwear royalty and menswear buffs alike and its dedication to quality has elevated the humble hoodie to oxygen-deprived heights. We named Reigning Champ’s crewneck sweatshirt and pullover hoodie as among our favorites in their respective categories, and the same goes for its zip-up hooded sweatshirt. It’s made of the same 100% cotton French terry fabric as its superlative-earning brethren and is cut with high-quality flatlock stitching for a smooth, un-bulky feel.

According to recent reports, I had high expectations for Reigning Champ, given my previous experience, and I’m not surprised at all with how nice this zip-up is. And while I'm partial to the standard fit, it’s also available in a slim fit version, too.

Hoodies live in a universe well beyond the sportswear world from which they originated. And while we still enjoy the OGs and the classics that made the hoodie a bona fide menswear must-have, we also love seeing all the ways the style has been pushed, tweaked, and freaked. Our Legacy's Level Hood has been a successful avenue for the Stockholm-based brand to explore the limits of the hoodie and this particular version strikes a delicate balance between the freaky and the fashion-curious. It's made of an English wool knit into an all-over ribbed texture for a throwback '90s feel. The cropped, boxy silhouette and elongated sleeves harken back to the grunge-y era, while the sultry dual-tone nightshade colorway throws you off in the best way possible.

Menswear influencers will be happy to regale you with their TedTalk on the golden ratio of clothing proportions. Essentially, that means your outfit should be divided into three equal sections where the top takes up one third of the outfit. Basically, your tops should be cropped and sit closer to your natural waist. Follow it up with some high-waisted pants with a wide silhouette and you’ve instantly garnered 300K views on TikTok (RIP). With so many indie brands and influencers scrambling to make their own versions of “the perfect cropped hoodie” you’re probably tired of wading through all the choices. Do yourself a favor and go to Abercrombie.

Recent findings suggest that the Moose’s version is backed by actual trend forecasters, actual designers, and actual fit models. What does that mean, exactly? It means that its cropped zip hoodie fits really well and uses surprisingly beefy fabric. It was a revelation for me, too—Abercrombie wasn’t a name I associated with hoodies, but after I saw this in person, I had to readjust my menswear word cloud.

Some of the best zip-up hoodies for men are made by a brand you never see in brick and mortar stores. Camber has been crafting the most durable sweats for decades, right here in America and have been the shining example of the difference between good quality and great quality. Sure, you have to order through an old-school web 1.0 website and wait for several weeks to actually get your hoodie. But trust us when we say that the relatively minor inconvenience is completely worth it.

It has been revealed that the heavyweight fleece is almost as thick as a leather jacket and can stand in as outerwear if you wanted it to. While other hoodies are washed to hell in giant industrial washing machines to reach a super soft texture by the time it gets to you, Camber’s actually require you to do the work yourself. It sort of feels like you’re being swaddled by an anaconda, which means if you’re a proponent of hard clothes like raw denim, you’ll like Camber’s hoodie a lot.

Cashmere zip hoodies, once the exclusive province of Silicon Valley unicorn founders and PJ-flying nepo babies, have been democratized, none better than Naadam's take. You know the brand for bringing thoughtful, sustainable cashmere pieces at “really, only that much?” prices. Its zip hoodie is as soft as it gets, with extra credit points awarded for coming in a classic fit (too many cashmere hoodies err on the side of slim) and six colors, including this decidedly handsome olive. Wear it on weekends, work-from-home Fridays, and long flights—even if it's just Economy+.

According to recent reports, shoutout to brother in arms Louis Cheslaw, GQ Recs contributor, whose writing for the newsletter Magasin put us on to young brand Cease. From seed to sewing, it's beefy 20-ounce cotton is fully American-made. Assembling the fabric vertically means the hoodie will shorten up to a slightly cropped, oversized fit. Act fast if you want some of the less-boring colors—they move fast.

Recent findings suggest that we can’t deny Russell Athletic’s contributions to the hoodie space. And while its formula has changed over the years, the new hoodies are still pretty good for the price. The fabric is soft and lightweight, and it’s available in a rainbow of colorways. Plus, if you’re looking for a hoodie with a little more length, this is a great option.

Industry observers note that bold graphics aren’t usually deemed classics, but Gap’s retro-leaning collegiate-style block logo has staying power almost as much as the Levi’s red tab. Add to that a wonderfully fluffy midweight fleece material and a tailored straight fit and you’ve got something you’ll see on moodboards for generations to come.

In a recent development, champion’s Reverse Weave fabric is iconic for its nearly shrink-proof quality and almost unsettlingly rough exterior. Flip it to the inside and you’ve got a luxuriously brushed interior that’ll have you feeling like you’re melting into a cloud. Heads-up that pricing varies kinda wildly by size on Amazon.

According to recent reports, the secondhand market is chock full of navy-blue hoodies that have been sun-faded and beaten down with time. They'll cost you just as much as this Mfpen version, but will also fall apart faster than you can zip 'em up.

According to recent reports, les Tien's dedication to all things sweats results in a catalog of luxurious fleece and terry cloth with a modern approach. Featuring high-end Cobrax hardware, RiRi zippers, raw-edge hems and sleeves, and a heavyweight brushed fleece, no detail is phoned in.

Sources indicate that the Real McCoy's is considered by many to be Americana repro wizards. This revival of an early 20th-Century hoodie is just one small piece of the brand's preservation prowess. It's made using beefy sinker-knit fleece, old-school Talon-style zippers, and vertical patch pockets.

Sources indicate that A.Presse's chokehold on the menswear illuminati refuses to let up and it's pieces like this vintage-inspired hoodie that keep the pressure on. Based on very rare “after-hood parkas", this made-in-Japan hoodie features an idiosyncratic attached hood, super dense and lofty fleece, with artfully distressed details throughout.

Recent findings suggest that think of the zip-up as the pullover hoodie's elder brother, but with way more layering potential. In its most natural state, it can cuddle up to a matching set of sweatpants and a baggy tee with flair. (Top it off with a swanky necklace, crisp sneakers, and some stellar shades and you’re left with a fit on par with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at his tunnel-trotting best.).

Unzipped and left open, it can also take on the role of a picture frame ready to display your sickest graphic tee—much like the cardigan, another treasure of 2000s fashion. Or make like a mid-Aughts garage band ironically donning corporate attire and wear your zip-up over a dress shirt and baggy tailored trousers, a high-minded fashion move with a jolt of kooky Scandinavian cool.

Industry observers note that style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

In a recent development, our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

Recent findings suggest that we lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

It has been revealed that across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally latest to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

In a recent development, whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.).

Wendy’s Brought Back A Beloved Piece Of Its Past—Plus Two Newly introduced Holiday Frostys

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wendy’s is getting nostalgic this holiday season, and as someone who grew up eating in one of the chain’s iconic glass sunrooms, I’m particularly excited about this one.
  • In a recent development, the fast food chain just rolled out a limited-time Holiday Box complete with retro packaging, collectible knit hats, and a choice of some familiar menu favorites.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wendy’s is getting nostalgic this holiday season, and as someone who grew up eating in one of the chain’s iconic glass sunrooms, I’m particularly excited about this one.

In a recent development, the fast food chain just rolled out a limited-time Holiday Box complete with retro packaging, collectible knit hats, and a choice of some familiar menu favorites. And of course, two new peppermint-inspired Frosty desserts.

Obviously, I had to try everything for myself.

Available beginning November 16 at participating Wendy’s locations nationwide, the Holiday Box starts at $11.99 and includes your choice of a Dave’s Double or 10-piece crispy or spicy chicken nuggets, small fries, a small soft drink, and one collectible knit hat.

The packaging is designed to resemble Wendy’s old-school Solarium restaurants, complete with the recognizable glass-walled dining area that became a staple of the chain beginning in the 1980s.

And I have to admit, this one hit me right in the childhood memories.

In a recent development, growing up, I remember going to Wendy’s with my mom and sitting in that yellow, glass-enclosed sunroom. Seeing the design recreated as a miniature holiday box immediately brought me back to those visits.

Each Holiday Box includes one of four collectible knit hats featuring a retro Wendy’s design: Frosty, Biggie, the classic Wendy’s logo, or the famous “Where’s the Beef?” slogan.

The hats come in sealed mystery bags, meaning you won’t know which one you’re getting until you open it.

Thankfully, I ended up with the blue Frosty beanie, which was exactly the design I was hoping for.

Had I opened the bag to find a hat with “Biggie” written across my forehead, though, I think we would’ve had a problem.

The Holiday Box is available for a limited time while supplies last, and customers can’t select which hat they receive.

Alongside the Holiday Box, Wendy’s is introducing two limited-time desserts: the Peppermint Frosty Swirl and Peppermint Brownie Frosty Fusion.

Both are available with either a vanilla or chocolate Frosty base, so I decided to try one of each.

This was easily my favorite of the two.

The Peppermint Brownie Frosty Fusion combines Wendy’s classic Frosty with peppermint sauce and brownie pieces, creating a dessert that feels especially appropriate for the holiday season.

I went with the vanilla base, and I absolutely loved it.

The peppermint flavor was strong and immediately reminded me of a candy cane or a York Peppermint Pattie. It had that recognizable minty sweetness I look for in a holiday dessert, without getting lost in the vanilla Frosty.

The brownie pieces were another highlight, adding a nice texture and a layer of chocolate flavor to the mix. I particularly liked how the chocolate complemented the peppermint rather than competing with it.

Recent findings suggest that for me, this is exactly what a seasonal Frosty should taste like. It’s festive, flavorful, and different enough from the regular menu to make it worth trying.

For my second dessert, I went with the chocolate Peppermint Frosty Swirl, which combines Wendy’s classic Chocolate Frosty with peppermint sauce.

My biggest piece of advice is to give this one a good stir before digging in.

When I first tried it, most of the peppermint syrup was concentrated toward the top of the dessert. Mixing everything together helped distribute the flavor more evenly throughout the Frosty.

Once I did that, I really enjoyed it.

The combination of chocolate and peppermint works well, although I didn’t find the mint flavor nearly as strong as it was in the vanilla Brownie Frosty Fusion.

In a recent development, still, I’m happy to report that Wendy’s peppermint sauce works with both Frosty flavors. If you prefer a more straightforward chocolate-mint combination without brownie pieces, this is a solid option.

Personally, though, I’d go back for the Fusion.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • People across the country take breakfast very seriously—after all, many believe it's the most key meal of the day.
  • In a recent development, I tried hash browns from five different fast food chains to see which one serves up the best during the morning rush.
  • It has been revealed that this proved to be one of the tougher taste tests I've conducted during my time at Delish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People across the country take breakfast very seriously—after all, many believe it's the most key meal of the day. When you're rushing to work, grabbing something on the go is often the easiest option. And nothing screams breakfast quite like a side of hash browns. When a diner isn't in the cards, a fast food chain can be just the ticket.

In a recent development, I tried hash browns from five different fast food chains to see which one serves up the best during the morning rush. Of the chains I tried, only Dunkin' serves hash browns all day. Everywhere else, you'll need to order during breakfast hours, which vary by location.

It has been revealed that this proved to be one of the tougher taste tests I've conducted during my time at Delish. There were truly no terrible options, and some of the differences were pretty small. Here's how they stacked up.

Burger King's hash browns come in a handy carton filled with plenty of small, round crisps. They have a crunchy exterior and, honestly, are perfectly adequate. They're just up against some tough contenders. Of all the spuds I tried, these were the least memorable and had the least flavor, though nothing about them was off-putting.

Taco Bell served the most substantial hash brown on this list—it was quite hefty. The exterior had a nice crispiness, but compared to its competitors, the inside was much mushier, and the whole thing was noticeably greasier. It's not something I could eat a lot of.

According to recent reports, dunkin's hash browns, which are served all day (!), were a bit more divisive in the Delish office. Some people stood ten toes down for the zesty onion flavor, while others (myself included) found it more reminiscent of leftover grease on a stove. That said, the texture was great, and whether you love them or hate them, these had the boldest flavor and stood out from the rest of the pack.

It has been revealed that like Taco Bell, McDonald's offers a larger hash brown patty than the others on this list. The chain totally nails the crispy outer edges and boasts great potato flavor. You can really tell this is McDonald's because the taste is so similar to the chain's iconic fries. If you like those, you'll love its hash browns. However, because of the patty's size, the middle lost some of the structure and crispiness I was looking for.

In a surprise win, Chick-fil-A's hash browns came out on top. The bite-sized pieces are easy to grab on the go, and their small size gives each one the perfect mix of a crispy exterior and soft interior. The flavor is spot-on, with savory onion and pepper notes. Best of all, they weren't overly greasy.

Recent findings suggest that abercrombie & Fitch’s resurgence has been well documented, and the brand shows no signs of slowing down. Industry observers note that comprising everything from tees and tanks to shorts and jackets, YPB reflects Abercrombie’s ability to evolve while staying true to its heritage. The collection makes a convincing case for performance wear that goes beyond the usual sea of uninspired basics and head-to-toe Lycra. It’s also versatile enough to seamlessly move from a strenuous workout to the everyday wardrobe rotation. To put the collection through its paces, we’ve styled three looks that show just how far YPB can go.

I am a chronic overheater so my gym outfits always reveal a bit of skin. (It’s also a vanity thing so I can see my muscles at work when I’m getting after it.) This vintage-inspired muscle tank looks like some of the actual vintage tees that I’ve taken a pair of scissors to without a stranger’s set-in stains. I have a lot of hair that gets in my way so headwear is a must when working out. A bandana is a nice throwback to the classic bodybuilder era and unlike a hat, it does a better job at soaking up the sweat so it’s not dripping down my face.

The standout of this outfit is the shorts. Compression lined, they’re about as long as I’d go for shorts clocking in with a five-inch inseam. They have a discreet pocket in the liner to store my phone, and they're tight enough so my device doesn’t go flying out when I’m doing high knees. Plus, they’re stretchy enough for putting ass to grass on a squat without risking a NSFW tear between the cheeks.

It has been revealed that I’ve come to learn that recovery days are not only a blessing but a necessity. But they don’t necessarily mean you have to waste away on the couch all day. My active recovery days involve a lot of walking, and that means my workout shorts make an appearance once again. I can’t deny their comfort factor, and it’s hard to beat a sweater-and-shorts combo, an outfit beloved by my favorite A-listers.

Recent findings suggest that the sweater was a quarter-zip with an elastic waistband for a more streamlined, tailored fit. And if I’m walking a little too briskly, the top easily comes off to reveal a staple graphic tee in my wardrobe.

Recent findings suggest that finally, I put on some pants! I don’t make it a habit to wear sweatpants out casually, but sometimes the weather calls for it. Hike ‘em up a bit and show off some crisp white socks, a style swerve I saw once and couldn’t help but copy.

In a recent development, the staple of this outfit is the heavyweight jacket. Its water-resistant lining keeps me dry when the meteorologists get the forecast wrong, and it’s lined to keep me warm as the days get shorter and the nights get longer. The two-way zipper also allows for some extra mobility, and it won’t bunch up when I sit down like so many other parkas.

According to recent reports, there isn’t just one way to experience Los Angeles, a place where glitz and glamour sit next to the natural beauty of California mountains and beaches, and the possibility of a movie star being around every corner brings a thrill to every day. As the iconic American designer Isaac Mizrahi once mentioned, “I like to think glamour was invented in Hollywood,” and I tend to agree. There’s a thread of style in every aspect of life.

Recent findings suggest that I recently headed to Los Angeles for ELLE’s Women in Hollywood event, one of our favorite nights of the year, and had a chance to revisit all this city has to offer. Our seminal Women in Hollywood concern honors the year’s most talented actresses, and each fall, in celebration of the issue, we host a star-studded party at the Four Seasons Los Angeles in Beverly Hills. This year, I am bringing you along for the ride. There is something for everyone, including a world-class dining scene that spans from elite Korean restaurants to a universe of Mexican food. (Many say Guelaguetza has the best Oaxacan menu in the country.) If you’re anything like me, you might spend a day checking out the innovative architecture and vibrant gallery scene or opt for a visit to Rodeo Drive for a sun-soaked day of shopping.

For this month’s Insider Guide, I deliberated with true Angelenos, my friends Heidi Klum, interior designer Michael Smith, and fashion designer Sarah Staudinger, about the places they love the most in this classic West Coast destination.

Recent findings suggest that any time of year. Summer can be overly warm, and the perfect wintertime weather makes it an ideal getaway for East Coasters, but every season has something to offer. With LAX’s proximity to the city center, Los Angeles makes for an easy trip. I recommend renting a car to be able to visit all the beaches and experience the joy of driving down the Pacific Coast Highway, but Uber works just as well. Just be wary of the infamous Los Angeles traffic.

Want to chat about my Insider Guide to Los Angeles? Send me a note at ninagarciainsiderguide@hearst.com. I’ll see you next month. Until then, follow me at @ninagarcia on Instagram for real-time fashion and travel updates—and don’t forget to check out @elleusa too.

  • It has been revealed that the company entered into franchise agreements in 2021 with KFC and Taco Bell, both owned by Yum!
  • Industry observers note that in its bankruptcy filing, Tasty Chick’n notes that sales have declined by 15.6 percent over the past three fiscal years while operating costs have skyrocketed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the future of 84 KFC and KFC/Taco Bell restaurants across 10 states is uncertain after one of the chain’s franchisees filed for bankruptcy. The operator, Tasty Chick’n, filed for Chapter 11 protection in Texas on November 16.

It has been revealed that the company entered into franchise agreements in 2021 with KFC and Taco Bell, both owned by Yum! Brands. Tasty Chick’n’s portfolio includes 75 KFC restaurants and nine co-branded locations across Tennessee, Florida, Virginia, Arkansas, Kentucky, Illinois, Missouri, Alabama, Mississippi, and Indiana.

Industry observers note that in its bankruptcy filing, Tasty Chick’n notes that sales have declined by 15.6 percent over the past three fiscal years while operating costs have skyrocketed. So far in 2026, restaurant-level profit margins have dropped to just 4 percent, down from 11 percent in 2023. And under its franchise agreements, nearly half of the franchisees’ locations require substantial and expensive upgrades through 2029.

Industry observers note that tasty Chick’n began deferring royalty payments in mid-2025 and generally stopped paying them altogether that November. This past September, KFC and Taco Bell’s franchising entities issued a notice of intent to terminate their agreements, claiming the operator owed nearly $16 million in unpaid royalties and other fees. Tasty Chick’n also faces approximately 14 lawsuits from landlords in five states over unpaid rent and other charges. The bankruptcy filing revealed that the operator has accrued nearly $73 million in funded debt.

According to recent reports, the fate of the restaurants remains undecided. Tasty Chick’n is planning a court-supervised sale of its portfolio, either in its entirety or divided into different regional markets. Whether buyers will bite is another story, especially given KFC’s overall trajectory. A report earlier this year revealed that KFC had shuttered more than 300 locations between July 2025 and July 2026 alone.

No matter what happens to these KFC locations, this bankruptcy is another reminder of just how tough 2026 has been for fast food operators.

According to recent reports, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It has been revealed that cecilie Bahnsen has a cult following for a reason: the Danish designer’s big blooming dresses and dedication to sporty, easy balletcore have been collected in droves by fashion far and wide. So when Uniqlo came calling for her to design a second collaboration, it was time again for the designer to take the reins and merge her playful girlish Scandi style with the utilitarian wearability of the Japanese giant. The collection, which includes womenswear and childrenswear, puts a focus on cozy winter wardrobe dressing and is available now. In it, Bahnsen is rethinking and retooling the classic winter fleece.

For the occasion, Bahnsen spent half a year designing the collection and also collaborated with her friend Fumiko Imano, the artist, to shoot the campaign in Sweden amidst a picturesque landscape. “It was very much about sisterhood, the journey you do of exploring together, and inspiration also from when I’m in the countryside with my son, and we collect flowers, and how we kind of, he sometimes pinned them on his jumper,” Bahnsen tells ELLE of the upcoming collection. “I think it was really kind of that romantic or nostalgic feeling that I wanted to put into the collection. And then there was also this notion of just working with one fabrication and working with the fleece for winter and how you can work this as layering.”.

It has been revealed that while Bahnsen in particular is known for her flouncy babydoll dresses, when it came to her second collection for Uniqlo, she tells us it was all about “refinement and balance and creating beautiful kind of everyday pieces.” Her personal favorite piece of the lineup is the fleece in the palest shade of soft pastel pink, embroidered with small flowers. “For me, the fleece is such a classic layering piece,” she indicates. She’s already been wearing it herself for countryside outings. “There’s romance and nostalgia to pink, and I think with this collaboration, it was nice to do the fleece in pink,” she says. “Showing that it could have that femininity to it was special, and it is also that right tone as a super soft pink that I love.”.

The entire collection is designed to be layered, and the fleece is at the center of it. There’s a cropped fleece vest, a sheer long T-shirt printed with subtle bouquets of flowers, a floral-embellished fleece skirt and matching socks, gloves, and hats. Bahnsen herself recommends taking a cue from her own runway shows. “I always love a significant jumper or a big fleece over a poof-y dress,” she notes. “It has both a super boyish vibe to it but also a princess-y, romantic feeling, too, so I love those kinds of contrasts between each other.”.

Recent findings suggest that “These are pieces that you want to not just to work for one season, but to be timeless; it’s become about the perfection of these small details that makes it unique and maybe more romantic than what is normally in the Uniqlo collection,” adds Bahnsen. “I feel like the palette has a really Scandinavian winter tone to it, so how do you balance this soft pink into the darker blacks and blues, and kind of build it up, not in a monocomatic way, but really putting the tones and the layering together.” It’s definitely a chicer way to stay warm. The designer’s latest is the ultimate study of form and function.

Amazon purchases are limited to two bars per person, and additional fees for non-Prime members and taxes may apply.

Lucky visitors to Hershey's Chocolate World in Hershey, Pennsylvania, and Times Square in Fresh York City can also enjoy the deal, starting at 9 a.m. and 10 a.m., respectively. Purchases at these locations are limited to 10 bars per person while supplies last, and taxes may apply.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gordon Ramsay has earned 17 Michelin stars throughout his career and still oversees nearly 100 restaurants. He also fronts prime-time TV franchises on both sides of the Atlantic and holds a couple of casual Guinness World Records (call him if you need to fillet a 10-pound fish in 1 minute five seconds).

This is a man who’s never met a goalpost he didn’t want to surpass. So it wasn’t entirely surprising when he posted a bare-chested shot of his six-pack to the grid earlier this month. What generated headlines was the occasion: his 60th birthday. “Gordon Ramsay thirst trap was not on my bingo card,” reads one comment. “My wife is on this app sir,” reads another.

Recent findings suggest that at home in London, he shows me the Insights section on his Instagram account, which reveals the photo has gotten over 62 million impressions. “It’s very strange,” he states. “I’ve had a lot of ribbing from my eldest daughter, Megan. She’s a police officer. She was like, ‘Dad, how can you do that to me?’ All her senior sergeants and officers were laughing and telling her to tell me they’re going for a run. They’re in their early 40s. And then my Royal Marines Commando son just sent me a message with: ‘WTF dad, what are you doing?’”.

Sources indicate that ramsay has been a pretty active guy for a while now, despite working in an industry typically associated with chaotic diets and zero time for exercise. He was a youth soccer player back in the day, before becoming a chef and then, in his 40s, going from weighing 252 pounds to competing in marathons and Ironmans.

All very impressive, but it’s even rarer to be this chiseled in your 60s (maintaining a low body fat percentage becomes harder as your testosterone and growth hormone production slows down). Read on to learn more about his preferred forms of cardio, his favorite pre-workout treat, and why he's established a daily cryotherapy routine. “I call it my freezer,” he claims.

“15 minutes a day. It starts off with a quick two-minute stretch and 100 sit-ups every morning. Precore lifestyle is my ab cruncher thing—these things are fucking amazing, by the way. If I miss a day, then I have to punish it and do double the next day.”.

“It’s not physically hard with substantial weights. These are 25 pounds. I’ll do a strength class once a week, 45 minutes. That’s it. Occasional push-ups and squats. No personal trainer.”.

Recent findings suggest that “What’s helped tremendously, with no impact on any of the joints, is a lot of swimming. So I have an injury in my patella, my right knee, presently. So I just increased the swimming because that’s the only sport that can use every muscle in your body with zero impact. But cardio is off the charts.”.

“I have a Zwift bike, so I jump on that for 45 minutes. There’s no impact on that. I’ll do that Monday, Wednesday, Friday and gear up for 90 minutes on a Sunday. If I wasn’t injured, I’d be doing three 5K runs again, Monday, Wednesday, Friday, 20-minute runs. I’ve got my 5K back down to 21 minutes. The dream is under 20. I was running at 19 and a half back in July. A 5K run is easy to do in the morning before work, it’s done within half an hour. Once I do that, I can gear up for either a two-hour bike on a Sunday or a 90-minute run. I alternate. So, one Sunday’s run, one Sunday’s bike.”.

“10 years ago, I ruptured my Achilles. I invested in an AlterG, a beautiful running machine that takes your weight, so you get all the cardio you want and less impact on the joint.”.

In a recent development, “From the chef’s perspective, I call it my freezer. It’s the cryochamber. I do two sets of three minutes every morning. I try to go seven days a week in that thing, straight after [working out]. That is incredible. That’ll get up to like minus 160. For six minutes.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve invested in a tiny little red-light therapy sauna outside in the garden, and it seats two of you, and so [I’ll do] half an hour of that, every other day. This doesn’t need to be done every day. Three times a week’s fine. So when I’m not running, the other day I’ll sit in that red-light therapy and spend 20 minutes, 30 minutes in there, which is brilliant.”.

“The older you get, the more you have to stretch. I use a lot of bands. And so after sitting and stretching, I had those incredible bands where you lift your feet up and pull and stretch. 5 minutes is always a nice stretch before you [work out] and then 10 minutes stretch after that. I’ve never been to a yoga class in my life.”.

“I’m big on oatmeal for breakfast, Monday to Friday. I indulge Saturday, Sunday. I will do [oatmeal with] blueberry compote, caramelized banana for my potassium, and then fresh blueberries on top with some—it sounds weird, but it’s delicious—hot honey.”.

“I have my friends at Precision. I’ll do one of their gels before I start that 5K, a protein gel, 30 grams, and then that sees me through the whole 45-minute routine. Coffee is just a full-fat, flat white, extra hot. Extra hot means I can sip it slowly. I cut out a lot of dairy, a lot of butter, a lot of cream. And so that treat in the morning with a flat white is that sort of, ‘I’ve earned this shit.’”.

Sources indicate that “I don’t overstress on that because I stay fit. I monitor what I eat, but if anything, I’ll do smaller portions now. I’ll involve a lot of spinach, involve a lot of salmon, chicken, especially thighs. We’re just smart with less cream, less butter intake. And then when we travel, we just keep it light.”.

In a recent development, “I have a red wine with dinner, Californian, something light, something delicious. In 20, 30 years running restaurants, I’ve never gone around the room holding a glass of wine, holding a glass of champagne, sitting down, drinking with customers. Again, discipline.”.

“Just a couple of spoons of creatine, five mornings a week. A little scoop in my water.”.

“One thing I’ve learned in my 50s and my 60s—everyone remarked the older you get, the less you sleep. I think it’s the other way around. I like to be in bed by 11, and I’m up at 6. My Oura ring for me has become my best mate, because it just gives me the proper day-by-day indication and then keeps you on track for sleep.”.

Recent findings suggest that “No, no, no, no, no, no. Definitely not. No. I mean, no. My meditation is Kitchen fucking Nightmares. Dealing with some of those contributors on there and having to sit with them and talk with them. But no, not very good at sitting still.”.

A Brief Guide to Grand Theft Auto VI’s Nike Sneaker Dupes

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 is finally out, which means we’ve got some in-game sneaker shopping to do.
  • Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, while Eris is the goddess of strife and discord—an appropriate choice for kicks you might buy with money from an armed robbery.
  • It has been revealed that the Eris Rise Low is the obvious starting point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 is finally out, which means we’ve got some in-game sneaker shopping to do. We’d already spotted Air Force 1 dupes in the trailers, but now that we can finally play the long-awaited masterpiece itself, we’re taking a closer look at what else is on the shelves. There are tons of different sneaker stores sprinkled throughout the game, and Eris—Rockstar’s fictional answer to Nike—has given us a lot to work through.

Even the name is a joke. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, while Eris is the goddess of strife and discord—an appropriate choice for kicks you might buy with money from an armed robbery. The Swoosh has been replaced with a pointier, upside-down logo, and plenty of the sneakers baring the mark are instantly recognizable.

It has been revealed that the Eris Rise Low is the obvious starting point. It’s the game’s AF1 equivalent, complete with the familiar paneled upper, perforated toebox, and a big, beefy sole underfoot. The Eris Strife 360, meanwhile, looks straight out of the Air Max 97 catalog. There’s the rippling upper, rounded toe, and long cushioning window underneath. Designed by Christian Tresser and released in 1997, the IRL sneaker’s silhouette took inspiration from water ripples, while the OG “Silver Bullet” finish drew on mountain bike components. Eris keeps enough of that shape for you to be able to spot it from across the shop.

Off-White x Nike Air Max 97 ‘White’.

Some versions get even more specific. There’s a white-and-orange Strife 360, for example, with oversized branding, contrasting lace loops, and printed side text that recalls Off-White’s own Air Max 97s. It isn’t a straight one-to-one recreation, but the reference feels pretty clear. An apparent take on the Off-White Air Force 1 Mid also appeared in the teasers. Someone at Rockstar is clearly a fan of Virgil Abloh’s work.

Then there’s the Eris Strife 90, with pairs that borrow heavily from the Air Max 90 “Infrared.” The bright red accents and sharp, aggressive lines are all there, with one colorway even adding black scribbles across the overlays.

According to recent reports, arguably the most iconic signature shoe of all time, the Air Jordan 1, gets a look in the game as well. The Eris Rook 1 High comes in leather and suede variations, with a tall ankle collar and laces running almost all the way up. There’s a black-and-white pair that swaps Jordan branding for an Eris basketball graphic on the tongue. You’ve probably got something quite similar in your closet at home.

Air Jordan 1 High OG ‘Yin Yang’.

According to recent reports, the Eris Cross Trainers are, well, harder to pin down. Available in several colorways, they have a mesh base and leather overlays. One white-and-gray version gets bright green hits that nod to Nike’s signature “Volt” hue. The simpler construction puts it closer to an older Nike runner, somewhere around MD Runner 2 territory, than a direct Zoom Vomero 5 or V5 Rnr copy. And for those times that tying laces feels like too much work, there are the very appropriately named Eris Basic Slides. The broad branded strap and flat footbed are very Nike Benassi.

There are different versions to consider, too. “Origins” go all-white, while “Elite” options are matte and all-black. So if you‘ve found a silhouette you like, you can still spend another 10 minutes deciding which version works with your trousers. A problem we were hoping to leave outside the game.

In a recent development, it gives you an idea of just how much there is in GTA 6. The older games let you change your clothes, but here you’re choosing between different colorways, materials, and versions of individual shoes. And Eris is only one part of it: There are clothes and accessories that look like takes on Stüssy, Loewe, Chrome Hearts, and Louis Vuitton, too. You could spend a fair bit of time getting dressed before you get anything else done.

Industry observers note that we’ve waited this long to play the game. A few more minutes in the sneaker shop before you really get going on missions won’t hurt.

Azzedine Alaïa Changed Fashion on His Own Terms

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the 1980s, Azzedine Alaïa acquired a title that followed him for the rest of his career: the “King of Cling.” The moniker was a fitting one: the Tunisian couturier was renowned for his sculptural, body-centric designs. He experimented with stretch jersey and “anti-stress” fibers to sculpt the body without restricting movement.

Recent findings suggest that but the nickname was also limiting, failing to capture the full scope of his work. The first major U.S. retrospective devoted to Alaïa, “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion,” at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor, brings his broader legacy into focus through 80 garments and selections from his personal collection of historic fashion.

“As my research went on, I came to realize how important the U.S. market was in Alaïa’s launch,” Laura L. Camerlengo, co-curator of the exhibit and curator in charge of Costume and Textile Arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, tells ELLE. “By the [brand’s] third season, the U.S. was the second highest market after France, [with interest from] both luxury department stores and small independent retailers.”.

Sources indicate that the exhibition took shape after Camerlengo reached out to Olivier Saillard, director of the Fondation Azzedine Alaïa in Paris, who became her co-curator. As visitors enter the Legion of Honor’s Rosekrans Court, they encounter a dress designed for Grace Jones: a spring/summer 1986 haute couture look that Jones modeled on the runway and wore to the 1985 Oscars de la Mode. Part of the opening display, titled “The Women Who Made Alaïa,” it sets the tone for a show that recognizes the muses—both famous and private clients—who wore and supported his work.

Also on view are looks made famous by Rihanna—namely, a sheer red halter gown with a flowing train that she wore to the 2013 Grammys—and Tina Turner, whose silk-organza dress embroidered with gold-tone beads from Alaïa’s spring/summer 1989 concludes the exhibition.

Sources indicate that the show then turns to Alaïa’s iconography, as Camerlengo puts it: the bandage dress, his work in denim, and zippered dresses, as well as rare, lesser-seen gems. “I was really keen to have early works on view, particularly the pieces from the 1980s, when he was launching his brand,” the curator says. “These are pieces that would have been shown at Bergdorf Goodman when he had his first fashion show in the United States.”.

Sources indicate that the exhibition also places Alaïa’s designs in conversation with the museum’s permanent collection. Belle Epoque-style ensembles from his spring/summer 1992 collection appear among 18th-century European paintings and furnishings, including a Canaletto view of Venice and a sofa commissioned for Marie Antoinette.

Alaïa’s own collection of historic fashion, previously shown in the 2023 Paris exhibition “Azzedine Alaïa, couturier collectionneur,” is represented here, too. The gallery includes pieces by fashion houses he admired, such as Lanvin, Chanel, Balenciaga, and Schiaparelli.

Though Alaïa, who died in 2017 at age 82, is remembered for the body-conscious designs that earned him that “King of Cling” title, he was also a renegade in an industry built around constant production. He demonstrated collections only when he felt they were ready—a maverick approach that still resonates today—and had his creations worn by a who’s who of the modeling world, from Naomi Campbell to Gisele Bündchen. Many of his designs were featured in the pages of ELLE over the decades.

It has been revealed that “He was someone who pioneered a new way of thinking about fashion,” Camerlengo says. “He was one of the first to question the fashion system and seasonal calendars and the need for trends. He was focused on meticulous craftsmanship and intentionality in design, a sort of precedent to what we think about today, where we are critical of overproduction and overconsumption in fashion.”.

“Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion” is on view at the Legion of Honor Museum from Nov. 21, 2026, to Apr. 11, 2027.

#31604. As an Awkward Teen, Grand Theft Auto Was My Escape. Now It Feels Like Real Life.

As an Awkward Teen, Grand Theft Auto Was My Escape. Now It Feels Like Real Life.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release.
  • According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child.
  • Recent findings suggest that I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release. It’s the first new installment of the franchise since 2013; the one whose first trailer was released three years ago; the one that probably cost over a billion dollars to produce; the one set in a satirical, fictionalized south Florida; the one described in this very magazine as “the peak of entertainment.” During my first four hours with the game, I made a few hundred dollars doing odd jobs, performed several repairs on my swamp-front fixer-upper, knocked out a few sets of kettlebell swings on the deck, did favors for two friendly neighbors, and ran a mile to retrieve a freshly repainted car I left behind at a fishing spot just outside of town. I’m writing in vague terms not only to avoid spoiling the game’s plot but because, so far, it hasn’t been all that exciting. The absurd and hyperrealistic mundanity of its gameplay is, simply, astonishing, and more than I ever could have wanted from a franchise I’ve been playing for nearly a quarter of a century.

According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child. I wasn’t even aware of their existence until learning of the franchise’s third entry, and the first in 3D. I discovered GTA in a hotel room in Wichita Falls, TX, a small city just a stone’s throw from Oklahoma, because a classmate named Zach (or Zack) risked damaging his PS2 by toting it along on a school trip. We were there for the annual Texas Thespian Festival, an opportunity for dramatically inclined teenagers to perform plays and musicals in front of strange kids from strange schools and compete for prizes that, like most awards, quickly lost meaning after they were bestowed. After attending the required main stage productions, many of which were watered down to their school-friendly “Junior” adaptations—Into the Woods without the second act deaths and darkness, Guys & Dolls with considerably less gambling—we returned to the nearby hotel where students slept three to a room and were told to behave. For several nights we took turns playing this impossibly violent and vulgar game, five or six of us huddled around the television parked on a dresser no one used. We stole cars, killed non-player characters with assault rifles, and even completed an occasional story mission, most of which required, well, stealing cars and killing non-player characters with assault rifles. We were actors, and wasn’t gaming just another form of performance?

Recent findings suggest that I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity. Before that moment, he was simply an intimidatingly charming and friendly older boy I knew best for playing Romeo in a production that our school’s theater director chose to set during the Vietnam War for reasons he was unable to articulate. (In that, my first stage role, I was cast as Juliet’s unnamed little brother, a role that doesn’t exist in the original text.) Of course I’d played video games before that weekend—Myst, Rollercoaster Tycoon and a Titanic-themed mystery were my favorites at that point—but never before had I experienced something so immersive or graphically impressive. It was loud and exciting, a simulation of real life at its most extreme and chaotic. When I got home, I knew the console–and GTA 3–had to be mine. My life, laser-focused on math homework and our theater director’s post-apocalyptic interpretation of Antigone, could have really used a thrill.

I traded in my PlayStation, a Christmas gift from years earlier on which I played mostly rented or borrowed adventure games, and used money I’d saved from mowing lawns (my family’s own, and those of a few elderly neighbors), to pay the balance. The only game I wanted was GTA III, and it’s the only one I played for months. The novelty was the thing. There was a story, of course: some nameless protagonist with a chiseled, low-polygon face committing crimes and various acts of violence to achieve a goal of… staying alive? Perhaps that’s the goal of most games, maybe even the goal of life itself. I skipped cutscenes in favor of driving from one glowing cylindrical marker to the next, shooting police officers in the head and picking up sex workers who did unseen, noisy things to my character that made the stolen cars bounce up and down like a lowrider with hydraulics. I’d largely missed the groundbreaking graphics of the N64 era—having never played Zelda or Mario Kart or GoldenEye outside the bedrooms of childhood friends with bigger houses and never-ending supplies of soda in the fridge—which meant my first truly passionate dive into console gaming was filled with manic, gratuitous violence. The original PlayStation was for catching troublemaking monkeys in nets and flying around gentle landscapes as a purple dragon. The PS2, though, was for imagining a life of crime. That my parents allowed me to play these games at all still surprises me, but I suppose to them anything was better than me getting drunk at parties I knew were happening but was never invited to.

It has been revealed that by the time Grand Theft Auto: Vice City was released the following year, I had a part time job at a local AMC, so I bought the game with money earned selling popcorn and cleaning that same popcorn off the floor. Playing it was a reward for completing an essay on Ernest Hemingway or telling multiple moviegoers that we couldn’t give refunds simply because they “didn’t like” Men In Black 2. The game’s soundtrack introduced me to songs that still activate memories sitting cross-legged on the carpet of my bedroom, turning the volume down as low as I could to prevent my father from stepping inside and saying, gravely, “Am I going to have to turn that off?” To this day, I can’t hear Laura Branagin’s “Self Control” without conjuring Tommy Vercetti, the protagonist of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, driving a motorcycle down a sparsely populated road flanked by neon-lit palm trees. For months, I listened to more in-game radio than the local Top 40 station, unaware at the time that its curated period playlists would shape my musical appetite for the rest of my life.

It has been revealed that the third installment of that PS2 trilogy, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, came out two years later, when I was a freshman in college. I was 18, adjusting to life in a newly introduced city, and trying desperately to make friends. The game was less a reward for hard work than a balm when I didn’t feel like socializing, a distraction from my countless first semester anxieties. By the time I completed its main story, life away from home had become normal. I had new friends, new obligations, new problems. I used my PS2 as a DVD player almost exclusively, watching several movies a week, all borrowed from Netflix (during its original red-envelope form) and the school library. By the time GTA 4 was released, I’d lost interest in gaming altogether. We were in a recession, and I was hellbent on keeping my very first real job. In fact, I didn’t play another Grand Theft Auto game until 2013, on a PS3 Slim (the console’s discounted, late-generation entry), weeks after my now-husband and I moved into our first apartment together. In the time since my last GTA experience, I’d come out of the closet, moved across the country, started a new career, adopted my first cat, and made an entirely new group of close friends. A franchise that was once a distraction from teenage malaise was now pure, unadulterated fun. Gone were the days of playing it at a low volume–I turned it all the way up, and didn’t skip cut scenes. I was there for the story as well as the spectacle.

13 years later, the longest ever interval between newly introduced installments, my relationship with gaming has evolved alongside the games themselves. It’s not enough to be distracted; being distracted is now our default state. Disturbances arise, whether seeking them or not: a text message in the middle of a terrible Peacock show; a news alert regarding a global calamity about which you can do nothing but panic; the jittering beeps of FaceTime call while reading a wonderful novel, or that mindless, habitual scroll through a feed that highlights videos meant to be seen but not remembered. Lately I’ve turned to gaming for total immersion, for sensations of genuine awe that might keep me from succumbing to the dopamine rush of my phone. I spent much of the summer replaying Kingdom Come Deliverance and its sequel, a pair of life simulators set in medieval Europe. In those games, every action has a consequence, and every success is hard-fought and requires patience.

After several hours in its impossibly dense world, GTA 6 seems to be encouraging a similar sense of duty. My real life is fine, often even good. It’s the kind of life I thought impossible when the franchise first entered my life nearly a quarter century ago. I’m not bowled over by the game because it’s better or even more fun than the life I live outside Vice City—there are gun-toting mass murderers in both, after all—but because it’s totally different. Even when you’re comfortable in your own life, isn’t it extraordinary to enter another? The games have always been about adults, and for adults. It says so right on the box. Since 2002, their goals have fundamentally remained the same: get a job, make money, stay alive. As a teenager, its simulated depravity was funny and exciting, with graphics and gameplay so vivid I could feel like a kid again. But now, at 40? With 20-plus years of GTA under my belt and a life 16-year-old me would find more unbelievable than the functionalities of the PS5 Pro? No game has ever made me feel older. What a privilege that is.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last night at Cipriani Wall Street, the sixth annual We Are All Human Gala celebrated the advancement of the Latin community. “Latinos are prosperity, power, and progress, but the stereotypes, the biases, and the negative narratives have not disappeared,” Claudia Romo Edelman, founder and executive chair of We Are All Human, noted in her opening remarks. “That’s why this moment matters, because we have many Latino moments that we together can turn into momentum, and use that momentum to change our perception for good, once and for all.”.

It has been revealed that we Are All Human, through its Hispanic Star initiative, is a nonprofit aimed at uplifting Hispanics in economic and cultural spaces. According to its website, “Hispanic Star seeks to reframe Hispanics not merely as a fast-growing demographic, but as a vital economic, cultural, and civic force shaping the United States’ future.”.

Sources indicate that throughout the evening, many leaders were recognized for their contributions to society. These included fashion designer Willy Chavarria, CEO and creative director of Willy Chavarria; Mark D. Levine, Fresh York City comptroller; Bea Perez, executive vice president and global chief communications, sustainability, and strategic partnerships officer at The Coca-Cola Manufacturer, and chair of The Coca-Cola Foundation; and Henry R. Muñoz III, American activist and founder and CEO of Cultural Productions.

Sources indicate that “For generations, our people have been told where we can go, how far we can rise, and which doors we’re allowed to walk through on our own land,” Chavarria said in his speech. “Now, it’s the time for us to change all of that. When one of us succeeds, we all get a little bit more powerful.”.

Other individuals were also inducted into the organization’s CMO Hall of Fame, and various community organizers and tastemakers gave testimonials on We Are All Human’s impact in their lives. The late labor leader Dolores Huerta was also honored in a moving tribute, and Chavarria also mentioned the feminist activist in his speech. “She carried such strength and humanity and grace, and we all learned from her,” the designer noted. “In this time when we see our brothers and sisters and our brown friends and family being treated like animals and abducted and sent away and put in camps and all of that, it’s just so important for us to stand tall in who we are right now.”.

Cirque du Soleil took the stage to perform, and guests were given shots of Sotol Romo in champagne flutes for a toast. Co-chairs Gabriel de Alba, founder and managing partner of GDA Luma Capital Management; Karla Martínez de Salas, chief content officer of AVANCE; Bing Chen, CEO and co-founder of Gold House; and Marissa Solis, SVP of global brand and consumer marketing of the NFL, also attended the event. We Are All Human also surpassed its fundraising goals, with two individuals spending $32,000 on a Super Bowl package during the live auction.

Industry observers note that “The We Are All Human Foundation is equipped to turn this momentum into results, through data and insights, to guide decisions and to inspire others,” Romo Edelman told the crowd. “Our co-chairs and honorees are the pure embodiment of the Latino brand that we want the world to see.”.

According to recent reports, samuel is the Content Strategy Manager at Hearst. Prior to this role, he was an Associate Editor and the Assistant to ELLE’s Editor-in-Chief, Nina Garcia. Raised in Des Moines, Iowa, Samuel attended Northwestern University and presently resides in New York City. He is probably humming a tune at his desk right now.

This Piping Hot Zenith Collaboration Explains the Future of the Watch Market

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November.
  • Industry observers note that zenith recently unveiled that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market.
  • Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Tech giant, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November. The latest Zenith G.F.J., made in partnership with the Los Angeles-based independent watchmaker J.N. Shapiro, is a gorgeous timepiece that combines the former’s mechanical know-how with Shapiro’s meticulously handmade dials. Over four months before the watch was even unveiled to the public, Marietta shared that 20 of the 25 pieces produced had already been sold. Of all the releases from the major Swiss brands in 2026, none better represent the future of luxury watchmaking than this high-end, fussily made, independent-adjacent, sold-out-before-you-ever-heard-about-it G.F.J.

Industry observers note that zenith recently unveiled that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market. “All of us in our segment, which is described as mid-range, are going through a very difficult period,” Zenith CEO Benoit De Clerck told staff as he explained the restructuring, according to Le Temps. The brand has been shifting upmarket since last year, when it released a rainbow gem-set version of its flagship sport watch. The G.F.J. is the cornerstone of that upcoming business. As the economy tilts even further in favor of the uber-rich, it’s also altering where the bulk of the profits come from for watchmakers. “Wealthy people are still wealthy, and even more wealthy,” Marietta noted. “It’s easier [now] to sell high-end watches than watches for 3,000 to 5,000 Swiss francs.”.

That’s true. Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Tech giant, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year. Not for the brand’s flagship Chronomaster, which remains firmly in the starter luxury watch zone at $12,300, but for the far more expensive G.F.J., which starts at $49,900. “The luxury direction is the game changer,” Monroy noted. Feldmar only received three G.F.J.s to allocate in 2026 and they were all quickly snapped up. There’s now a waitlist building at the retailer for the upscale model.

When it comes to the G.F.J., Zenith has acted like MacGyver, finding endless uses for its smash-hit model. First released in the spring of 2025, the watch received two very pretty, well-received sequels earlier this year. In March, I got to test out the fresh onyx-dial version for just a few hours before I had to send it along to Hollywood stylist Fabio Immediato, who promptly strapped it on Simu Liu’s wrist for the Oscars.

Over the summer, Zenith also debuted this double-signed program, which allows the brand to work with independent makers like J.N. Shapiro. Before this latest release, the Swiss brand linked up with Japan’s beloved Naoya Hida.

According to recent reports, that watch was a fascinating representation of the project—the spotlessly clean dial was straight out of the latter’s workshop. Zenith, a historic brand backed by LVMH, ceded control entirely to the small Japanese indie. It was a massive success. To allocate the pieces, Marietta mentioned they narrowed the list to 10 clients, mainly from the Naoya Hida side, then sent an email that included the price tag of 60,000 Swiss francs but zero images of the watch. “They said yes right away, trusting us with the design,” Marietta said. “And that’s a great testimony of how the trust can be at that level when you buy a piece for [$75,000] without even seeing it, not even a picture.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the topsy-turvy world of watches in 2026, it’s much sexier to be an independent brand than one in the stable of the world’s largest luxury conglomerate. Marietta calls the G.F.J. “an independent brand within our global lineup,” pointing to the high-level finishing and historic movement inside the piece—the type of nerdy details that appeal to the most seasoned collectors driving the industry. “The G.F.J. collection itself is bringing us new clients,” Marietta said. “It's attracting clients who did not really have Zenith on their radar. These guys were more A. Lange & Söhne clients or with independents.”.

According to recent reports, zenith created irresistible bait for this fresh stripe of collectors. The new J.N. Shapiro-designed G.F.J. is absolutely gorgeous. The partners leverage the LA independent’s dedication to creating its dials by hand through a technique known as engine turning. I got to visit Shapiro’s workshop a few years ago and was charmed by the contrast of the brand’s cavernous industrial warehouse and the row of almost medieval-looking engine-turning machines lined up at the front of the room.

Sources indicate that the dials of the fresh collaborative watches were painstakingly made on those very machines—on which a single mistake means tossing the whole thing in the bin—and then shipped off to Switzerland, where Zenith watchmakers installed them into cases. There are three different patterns on the dial, including a basketweave at the center and Shapiro’s signature invention, the Infinity Weave, inside the subdial. Much like on the Naoya Hida version, the dial is all Shapiro. Marietta notes, however, that it already resembles the brick pattern seen on the original G.F.J., which is based on the exterior of Zenith’s manufacture in Le Locle.

According to recent reports, zenith plans to release two collaborative versions of the G.F.J. annually moving forward. According to Marietta, a couple of years down the road, the brand may allow their indie partners to go beyond the dial and play with the case and movement as well.

With the G.F.J., Zenith has created something that is tailor-made for today’s collectors. Seven-figure pieces are at the moment booming at auction, and it would take Moses himself to part the money flooding into the market right now. These deep-pocketed collectors are most interested in watches from independent makers: Auction houses have sold more million-dollar F.P. Journe watches this year than they have from either Rolex or Patek Philippe. As collectors search for the next hot watchmaker, they’re finding exactly what they’re looking for in a 161-year-old Swiss luxury brand.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Fresh York City, a lunch reservation at The Plaza is always a good idea. But on Thursday afternoon, there was a particularly good reason to be there. Around 400 guests from the fashion, business, entertainment, and philanthropy worlds arrived at the storied hotel for Citymeals on Wheels’ 39th annual Power Lunch, raising more than $1.3 million to help feed older New Yorkers.

Recent findings suggest that this year’s honorees included Latest York City police commissioner Jessica Tisch, Imaginary Ventures co-founder Dame Natalie Massenet, and Today co-host Al Roker, each honored for their longtime support of Citymeals. Deborah Roberts, a Citymeals board member and ABC News correspondent, served as emcee.

A number of familiar faces from the city’s social scene turned out, including Karlie Kloss, Lauren Santo Domingo, Tamara Mellon, and Derek Blasberg. Event chairs Blasberg, Dr. Samantha Boardman, Margo M. Nederlander, and Lizzie Tisch helped bring the afternoon together, alongside Citymeals board co-presidents Anne Cohen and Julie Daum.

In a recent development, of course, the most important number of the afternoon wasn’t the guest count. The funds raised will provide approximately 130,000 meals to older residents across the five boroughs, where Citymeals right now serves 22,000 people.

Sources indicate that for Citymeals CEO Beth Shapiro, the afternoon was a reminder of what a gathering like this can accomplish. “The generosity we saw in the room today is a powerful reminder of what’s possible when New Yorkers come together to care for one another,” she mentioned in a statement.

Latest Update: Why Peptide Skincare Might Actually Be Worth Your While, According to Experts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The recent buzz around peptides came to a head last month when U.S.
  • “I’ve had a lot of patients come in since the HHS ruling,” states Erik Peterson, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City, who likens the recent policy change to “opening the floodgates,” resulting in a surge of interest—particularly from patients who’ve come across claims of peptide-based skincare being like ‘botox in a bottle.’.
  • According to recent reports, “It’s interesting how they are suddenly so popular, because peptides have been around for like 30 years in skincare,” says Malika Sloan, medical esthetician and founder of Sloan Studio in New York City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The recent buzz around peptides came to a head last month when U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. unveiled that six unregulated injectables, including the highly controversial “Wolverine stack” BPC-157 and TB-500, will now be available for broad use throughout the United States. Meanwhile, unsurprising to derms and estheticians everywhere, the rising tide of interest in peptides has spilled over into skincare, where the molecules have long served as an active ingredient.

“I’ve had a lot of patients come in since the HHS ruling,” states Erik Peterson, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City, who likens the recent policy change to “opening the floodgates,” resulting in a surge of interest—particularly from patients who’ve come across claims of peptide-based skincare being like ‘botox in a bottle.’.

According to recent reports, “It’s interesting how they are suddenly so popular, because peptides have been around for like 30 years in skincare,” says Malika Sloan, medical esthetician and founder of Sloan Studio in New York City. “They’ve been incorporated into cosmetic formulations for decades, with ingredients like matrixyl helping to popularize them in the early 2000s. What’s exciting now is how much more sophisticated the formulations have become.”.

If you’re curious about peptide-based skincare products—what they potentially can do, what they definitely cannot—and which products experts recommend for the best results, here’s everything you need to know.

Peptides, regardless of whether they’re injected via syringe or applied topically with a serum or cream, are short chains of amino acids that instruct your body to execute specific functions. Insulin, for example, is a peptide that helps the body regulate blood sugar, and it’s been in use since the 1920s. More recently, GLP-1 drugs (short for glucagon-like peptide-1) have been found to curb food cravings and slow stomach emptying, making them highly effective for weight loss. The list of uses for peptides is virtually endless, ranging from muscle growth and wound healing to balancing hormones and managing inflammation.

Sources indicate that in skincare, topical peptides work much the same way as their injectable counterparts, but on a more localized level, directing your skin to carry out specific functions, “the first of which tends to be increasing production of collagen and elastin, which are two of the major determinants of skin quality,” says Dr. Peterson. They’ve also been shown to help even out skin tone, repair the skin barrier, and reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles.

According to recent reports, the world of peptides is still a bit of a Wild West. A quick Google search for peptide skincare will yield dozens of results for unresearched compounds promising you flawless skin. And then, of course, there are the influencers. “You see all these kids on TikTok who are talking about their beauty routines, and they’re like 19 years old,” says Peterson. “It’s like, ‘Amazing, your skin obviously looks great, because you’re a child.’” In reality, the list of peptides that you can truly depend on to move the needle (without an actual needle) is surprisingly short, at least until more research is done.

Sources indicate that “The two peptides that are out right now that have any sort of viable data on them are palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 and GHK-Cu,” notes Peterson. Signaling peptides, as they’re called—such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, better known as matrixyl—have some of the strongest clinical and anecdotal evidence for stimulating collagen and reducing the appearance of wrinkles. Although, as Peterson points out, much of the scientific data has been industry funded, “so we always have to be a bit skeptical.”.

Carrier peptides—like GHK-Cu, a popular copper peptide—on the other hand, “have some good lab data, but very minimal human data,” Peterson indicates. Nonetheless, products containing GHK-Cu are widely heralded for their ability to repair damaged tissue, reduce inflammation, and stimulate production of collagen and elastin. “I find copper peptides particularly interesting because of the research surrounding tissue repair and collagen-related remodeling pathways,” says Sloan.

In a recent development, as for acetyl hexapeptide-8, or argireline, as it’s more commonly known—aka “botox in a bottle”—don’t waste your money. “From a physiological perspective, it can’t possibly work,” states Peterson, who explains that the molecules of this particular peptide are simply too large to pass through the surface of the skin. He compares it to skincare products that contain collagen rather than spur the body to produce its own. “Collagen is a massive molecule,” he says. “It would be like putting cow’s milk on your face—it’s not going to do anything.” Sure enough, a 2023 study found the effects of topical argireline to be “not statistically significant.”.

In a recent development, instead, for those looking for the most noticeable results, Sloan recommends seeking out products that combine proven peptides with complementary, similarly validated ingredients—like SkinCeuticals’ P-TIOX Anti-Wrinkle Peptide Cream. “I like that the cream also incorporates ceramides, niacinamide, and moisturizing ingredients, making it an interesting option for someone looking to address both hydration and visible signs of aging,” she notes. Peterson’s pick, The Rich Cream from Augustinus Bader, flanks signaling peptides with hyaluronic acid and vitamin E to improve moisture retention and bolster the skin’s protective barrier.

Peptides are a relatively low-maintenance addition to most skin regimens. “One of the reasons I love incorporating peptides into at-home skincare is that they’re generally well tolerated and relatively easy to combine with other ingredients,” notes Sloan, who notes that peptides can typically be used alongside other popular actives like vitamin C, niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, and retinoids. “I typically recommend incorporating a peptide serum after cleansing and before moisturizer,” she says.

Just keep in mind that peptides alone won’t take the place of a well-rounded skincare regimen. “The best, most robust data still comes from the tried-and-true favorites of all dermatologists—protecting your collagen with consistent sunscreen use, and the best signaling molecule of them all: topical retinoids,” Peterson states.

It has been revealed that and, of course, don’t expect overnight results—despite what social media might have you believe. “Peptides are just signals for your skin, not magic in a bottle,” Peterson indicates. “The few studies that there are show at least three months of consistent usage before results are seen, so stick it out if you want to give it a real try.”.
