📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

According to recent reports, don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

“We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” says Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef stated.

Industry observers note that ursa began as a pop-up in El Centro, California, in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

After helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee states.

Industry observers note that consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez says. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”.

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a newly introduced planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

“We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee claims of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Recent findings suggest that ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

Recent findings suggest that “I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he indicates. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”.

Fall baking has a way of leaving you with awkward amounts of leftover canned pumpkin. So many recipes call for half a can or some other quantity that leaves you wondering what exactly you’re supposed to do with the rest. You put the open can of Libby’s pumpkin puree in the refrigerator with every intention of using it, yet a few days later, there it is, still waiting for you to come up with a initiative. It’s not as though you can make half a pumpkin pie.

Fortunately, you don’t need much pumpkin to make something wonderful. In fact, one of the best things I’ve made with leftover pumpkin requires less than a cup, a handful of pantry staples and very little effort. It’s the sort of recipe that makes having leftover pumpkin feel less like a nuisance and more like a stroke of good luck.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, these are a little different from the dense, chewy blondies you might be accustomed to. The recipe lists the chocolate chips as optional, though I’d argue strongly in favor of including them. The pumpkin blondies also almost suspiciously easy to make. Everything comes together in one bowl, using ingredients you probably already have on hand. There’s no frosting to fuss with, no dough to chill and no pie crust to negotiate. Just spread the batter into a 9-inch pan and bake it for 25 to 30 minutes. You’ll have a dozen soft, spiced bars that are equally at home on a Thanksgiving dessert table as they are next to your morning coffee.

Recent findings suggest that best of all, the recipe calls for just 1/2 cup of canned pumpkin. That’s a particularly convenient amount when you’ve got the remains of another baking project taking up residence in the refrigerator. And if you have a full cup left, making a double batch seems like a perfectly reasonable course of action.

Industry observers note that and there’s no reason to limit pumpkin to sweet recipes. A few spoonfuls can add body and richness to soups, pasta dishes and risotto, especially when paired with sage, garlic and Parmesan. Just be sure you’re using plain pumpkin puree rather than pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices and isn’t as versatile.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re not quite ready to commit to another pumpkin project, you can always freeze your leftover pumpkin puree. That way, the next time a recipe calls for an odd amount of pumpkin, you’ll have some on hand.

Industry observers note that if you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

Recent findings suggest that in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

In a recent development, to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

It has been revealed that if you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

Be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

For a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Industry observers note that because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

According to recent reports, but there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

If you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

You can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

In a recent development, soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Recent findings suggest that most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

Recent findings suggest that but we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

There’s more than one way to whip.

In a recent development, by hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

In a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

In a recent development, secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

It has been revealed that good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

You can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

Recent findings suggest that need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

Recent findings suggest that for something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

Industry observers note that in any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

Industry observers note that if your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

This is probably a temperature issue. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Recent findings suggest that another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

Industry observers note that even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from stated anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. It has been revealed that cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

It has been revealed that remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. It has been revealed that these Thanksgiving sandwiches make the most of what you’ve got, whether that’s a few slices of turkey or enough stuffing and cranberry sauce for an encore. Go all in with a gooey melt, load a pita with spiced turkey and crunchy vegetables, or give turkey the chicken salad treatment. There’s no need for post-holiday blues when a leftover turkey sandwich is on the horizon.

Industry observers note that give your Thanksgiving leftovers the club treatment by layering turkey and cranberry sauce with crisp bacon and lettuce. And don’t forget that middle slide of bread. We’re not animals, after all.

Need a break from heavy Thanksgiving fare but still have turkey to use up? Shred it, toss it with butter-bloomed spices, and tuck it into a pita with a bright, tangy slaw.

In this play on a turkey club, the middle slice of bread gets swapped out for leftover stuffing fried in bacon fat. (We repeat: stuffing fried in bacon fat.).

Turkey and cranberry sauce already have a salty-sweet thing going on. Why not play that up by swapping plain bread for custardy French toast?

In a recent development, sometimes it’s best to keep a leftover turkey sandwich simple. Turkey, cranberry sauce, cheese, and fresh sage, pressed until golden, give you all the flavors of Thanksgiving in four ingredients (plus bread).

According to recent reports, though the recipe calls for cooked chicken, you guessed it—you can swap in leftover turkey seamlessly. The apple and fennel both provide lots of crunch and freshness.

Recent findings suggest that another chicken banger that works beautifully with leftover turkey. Boosted with red curry paste, tangy from Greek yogurt, this mixture is as good stuffed into lettuce cups as it is tucked between sliced bread.

This recipe sticks close to the classic turkey club, with one simple twist: a punchy, verdant herb mayo that comes together in seconds in the blender.

Industry observers note that roast turkey, tangy sauerkraut, melty Swiss cheese, and a tangy sauce? Heaven. Bonus points if the rye bread you use is studded with caraway seeds.

#31466. Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

📅 28 Apr 2025 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (648 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Epicurious ↗ Open Full Page

Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

📅 28 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that these homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon.
  • Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp.
  • I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that these homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 issue of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

Industry observers note that turkey is the star of Thanksgiving dinner, but it can also be the star of dessert if you stretch your imagination enough. This idea first gained popularity on TikTok, using chocolate-dipped strawberries, marshmallows, pretzel rods, and melted chocolate to create these adorable little treats.

They're so simple to make: To make a leg, you spear two mini marshmallows with half a pretzel rod, then use kitchen shears to trim the edges into a long oval shape. Repeat for a second leg, then cut one mini marshmallow diagonally in half to make the wings. You'll stick these to the strawberry with a dab of melted chocolate (which acts as your glue), then let that sit to adhere. All that's left is a quick bath in melted chocolate.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

As an avid baker, I've been waiting for such a sturdy set.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Serious bakers will appreciate the hefty, high-quality materials in this 6-piece set. It's also gloriously nonstick.

When I got married a few years ago, I put a cohesive bakeware set on my registry to replace years of mismatched Goodwill finds. While it worked well for a few months, within a year it began to show serious signs of wear and tear. Baked-on grease stains, rust spots and even warping had me in the market for a fresh bakeware set much sooner than I expected.

Sources indicate that so, when I heard that my favorite cookware brand was releasing a bakeware set promising a sturdy, nonstick experience, I jumped at the chance to test it. Here’s everything you need to know about the new HexClad bakeware line, including my honest thoughts after two months of testing.

HexClad’s fresh hybrid bakeware set features six core pieces:.

It merges the benefits of stainless steel and nonstick into one easy-to-clean package. HexClad’s “hybrid technology” combines hexagonal steel peaks with nonstick valleys to improve heat circulation and release after baking. In other words, this bakeware browns your food evenly without it sticking to the pan.

Recent findings suggest that other features include ergonomic handles and a 2.5mm tri-ply construction to prevent warping. It’s also oven-safe up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit and dishwasher-safe. You can even use your favorite metal spatula or tongs without scratching the surface. And, like all HexClad cookware, it comes with a lifetime warranty against manufacturer’s defects.

Industry observers note that I’ll admit: I’m already a significant fan of HexClad. I reach for the brand’s skillets and knives daily, and I’ve hoped for years that they would release a bakeware line.

So, when the offer to test the new set landed in my inbox, I couldn’t say no. But would it live up to the hype I’d built up in my head? I put all six pieces through the paces for two months to find out.

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

Recent findings suggest that like all HexClad products I’ve tried, the bakeware packaging experience is impeccable. The set arrived securely in one big box, separated with foam. Each piece was also wrapped in a protective dust bag, which is a nice touch.

Immediately, I was awed by the construction of these pans. Just by touch, I could tell they were high quality. I grabbed my food scale to compare the weight of the HexClad pans to my go-to carbon steel pans. The HexClad options weighed more than twice as much as my existing bakeware. Talk about heft!

In a recent development, now, some folks might not appreciate that extra weight—especially since the pans get even heavier when full of food. But as someone who often replaces her bakeware every few years due to warping or rusting, I’m excited for a sturdier option. I hope this is the last set of bakeware I ever need to order.

As a final step, I washed each piece and got ready to bake!

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

One of my favorite things to make with sourdough discard is a massive loaf of focaccia bread, so that was a natural first test in the 13×9 HexClad pan. Focaccia dough is sticky, but a generous coating of olive oil helps prevent it from gluing to the pan. Still, after proofing and baking my bread as usual, I was impressed that the final product pulled slightly away from the pan’s edges, making it slide out with complete ease. The bottom and edges got nice and toasty brown, too.

A few nights later, I used the same focaccia dough to make a focaccia pizza. Same sticky dough, made even stickier with tomato sauce, cheese and toppings. Plus, since it’s such a rich dish, I cut back on the amount of olive oil I used. Despite all the add-ons, this focaccia baked and released from the pan just as beautifully as the first loaf.

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that next, I made a chocolate layer cake with the 9-inch round cake pans. Now, I’m typically a ride-or-die parchment paper user. I find cutting out perfectly sized parchment circles a tedious task, but it’s worthwhile insurance against my cakes sticking. But to truly put the HexClad pans’ nonstick properties to the test, I skipped adding parchment and simply greased my pans with a little butter and flour.

According to recent reports, after baking and 10 minutes of cooling came the moment of truth: Would it stick? Luckily, no! Both cakes released with minimal effort. I simply ran a butter knife around the rim of the cake before using the cooling rack to flip ’em out. It’s a good thing, too, because this was my dad’s birthday cake!

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

My nonstick tests continued with the 8×8 square pan when I whipped up a batch of candy bar blondies. These blondies used an assortment of leftover Halloween candy, so I thought for sure the caramel ooze from a Baby Ruth bar would cause some concerns. But nope! Even without parchment paper, treats slipped right out of the pan.

In a recent development, but how does HexClad bakeware perform with healthier treats? For one final test, I baked a completely made-up “brownie” recipe with pumpkin seed butter, applesauce, molasses and cocoa. It was a gooey, chocolaty mess by the time I put it in the pan, yet it baked and released beautifully.

Finally, I put the baking sheet to the test.

Now, I already own the HexClad pizza steel, which I use almost daily. It’s my go-to for everything from frozen pizza to galettes to roasted broccoli, and I find that it works even better than an air fryer to yield crisp, golden brown bakes. I’ve said on many occasions that it’s my all-time favorite piece of bakeware, especially for savory foods.

Both the pizza steel and baking sheet utilize HexClad’s tri-ply construction with an aluminum core and TerraBond nonstick coating. The former is a jet black colorway, while the baking sheet is gray.

Across the board, I found the baking sheet could handle every task I threw its way—including roasting a spaghetti squash. Oftentimes, I find myself scrubbing for what feels like days after roasting squash and scouring off that sticky, burnt-on residue. The HexClad pan cleaned with a simple swipe from a damp paper towel.

During testing, I found the bottoms and handles of the HexClad bakeware smudged a bit. After all, it is made of stainless steel. This didn’t bother me, and it was easy to clean by handwashing and drying it immediately. Over time, I may need to use a more abrasive regimen to clean stainless steel.

Industry observers note that while the HexClad pans are very sturdy, you should still let them fully cool before washing. Don’t throw a hot pan directly in the sink. The pans are also dishwasher-safe, though handwashing is recommended. (And honestly, so easy thanks to the nonstick coating.).

Across the board, I’m impressed with the latest HexClad bakeware line. I hope we see even more pieces in the future, like a muffin tin and loaf pan. Only time will tell exactly how it holds up, but from what I’ve experienced so far, this set really is designed to last a lifetime. (And I’ll be continuing to long-term test the set, and enhancement this review accordingly.).

Ready to take your bakes to the next level? This all-in-one set is great for beginners and pros alike.

You can shop the full 6-piece bakeware set on the HexClad website for $399. Select styles, like 2-pack sets of small and medium baking sheets, are also available.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Sources indicate that healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

20 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.).

Recent findings suggest that stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

#31461. Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (832 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tasteofhome ↗ Open Full Page

Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined.
  • I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone.
  • It has been revealed that imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Recent findings suggest that pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined. Here's how to know if your bird is safe to eat so you can stay calm and turkey on.

I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone. I wasn’t an experienced cook at the time, and it was one of my first attempts at making a Thanksgiving turkey. I used a helpful guide for how long to cook a turkey and even invested in a meat thermometer to be sure it reached at least 165°F. It looked great, and I was so proud!

It has been revealed that imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside. I was so nervous my guests would assume the turkey was undercooked. I didn’t know then that pink turkey can be perfectly safe to eat—as long as it’s cooked to that vital internal temperature.

Cooked turkey can look pink for a few reasons that have nothing to do with doneness, including the age of the bird, how it’s prepared and natural pigmentation.

Recent findings suggest that “Poultry naturally can have a pink hue,” indicates Heidi Diestel of turkey farm Diestel Family Ranch in Sonora, California. “The legs and thighs have more of the natural pigments that give meat its darker color. Those pigments, along with changes that happen during cooking, can leave some pink even when the turkey is fully cooked.”.

Sources indicate that the pigments Heidi refers to are proteins called myoglobin and cytochrome c. The more of these proteins the meat has, the darker it will be. Older animals tend to have more proteins, and therefore darker pigmentation, as do any regularly exercised muscles. That explains why leg meat is darker than breast meat, as turkeys spend the bulk of their days walking and running.

Cooking can also cause a chemical reaction with these proteins that contributes to a pink color. Smoked turkey often stays pink from the reaction of the meat to the smoke inside the grill or smoker, but even oven-roasted turkey can have a pinkish hue. Myoglobin usually turns white during the cooking process, but cytochrome c is more resistant to heat and can maintain a pink blush.

Grace Natoli Sheldon for Taste of Home.

Using a meat thermometer is the best way to know if your turkey is safe to eat.

Poultry is considered safe to eat when it meets a cooking temperature of at least 165°. However, the Taste of Home Test Kitchen recommends cooking the leg and thigh meat to 170° for the best texture. For stuffed turkeys, don’t forget to take the temperature of the stuffing as well, which should reach at least 165° when the thermometer is inserted in the center of the stuffing.

If your turkey comes embedded with a round plastic doneness indicator that pops when the turkey is ready, don’t use that as an absolute; they are notoriously inaccurate.

To check if the turkey is done, insert the thermometer in a thick, meaty area, making sure the tip doesn’t touch any bones (bone will show a higher temperature).

If you’re using a probe thermometer that you insert before cooking, double-check its position once the turkey has been cooking for a while. Meat contracts as it cooks, so it may no longer be in the best spot.

According to recent reports, if any part of your turkey is below 165°, you should continue cooking the turkey until all parts reach a safe temperature. It’s common for the thermometer to register different temperatures in different areas, since white meat cooks at a faster rate than dark meat. Don’t be tempted to cut off the parts that aren’t ready and return only them to the oven. It’ll increase the risk that undercooked juices will run onto your cutting board and contaminate the properly cooked turkey.

It has been revealed that if the legs and thighs aren’t done but the breast is, I like to baste the white meat and loosely tent it with foil to try and lock in as much moisture as possible. If the dark meat is ready but the breast needs more time, there’s no need to sweat it. Dark meat has enough natural fat and moisture that it won’t become dry with a little extra time in the oven.

It has been revealed that you should never knowingly eat undercooked turkey. According to the CDC, undercooked turkey can contain harmful bacteria, like Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens or Campylobacter, that can cause foodborne illnesses.

There’s also a risk of bacteria if the turkey isn’t thawed or prepared correctly. Give yourself plenty of time to thaw a frozen turkey, either in the refrigerator or in a cold water bath. Also, make sure to keep the counter or cutting board where you’re prepping the turkey clean and sanitized before and after handling the raw bird.
